sentences.text: Fossils of the genus have been recovered from Late Cretaceous rocks across many U.S. states, including the Kansas locality where this species was found.
Enchodus machairus is a newly described species of the fish genus Enchodus.
The species was named by Nelson, Murray and Sims.
Its type locality is the Niobrara Formation in Kansas, United States.
The prominent fangs, streamlined body and large eyes indicate a predatory lifestyle.
Fossilized stomach contents of larger predators frequently contain Enchodus remains, showing it was preyed upon by sharks, other fish, mosasaurs, plesiosaurs and seabirds.
Species are generally divided into a North American clade and a Mediterranean clade.
Enchodus machairus lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
Specifically, it inhabited the Coniacian to early Campanian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Species of Enchodus were abundant in Late Cretaceous marine ecosystems worldwide.
Limited evidence suggests some Enchodus may have survived into the Paleocene or Eocene, though this could represent reworked Cretaceous material.
The separation of North American and Mediterranean clades may reflect several isolated evolutionary events during the Late Cretaceous.
